vignette:
Miguel

Miguel was twenty-three when the men came. He had been working at a construction site outside San Salvador, saving money to bring his wife Rosa to the States, when a van pulled up and three uniformed officers dragged him into it. What happened over the next eighteen hours-the electrical cords, the questions about people he didn't know, the blows that came whether he answered or stayed silent-had left him with a scar along his ribs and a conviction that the world was fundamentally unsafe. He had escaped when a guard's attention wavered, and three years later, having rebuilt his life in Phoenix with a new job and a fresh start, he believed he had moved past it. Then the divorce papers came, and with them, a kind of unraveling he had not anticipated.

At twenty-six, Miguel now worked as a maid at a mid-range hotel, pushing a cart through corridors that smelled of bleach and old carpet. The job was steady, the pay modest but reliable, and it kept him occupied-or so he had thought. Everything changed the morning a silver sedan pulled into the parking lot, its shape and color too close to the van that had taken him. Miguel felt his chest tighten as he watched it from the laundry room window. That afternoon, unable to stop thinking about it, he found himself scrolling through news articles about kidnappings and police brutality in Central America, something he had trained himself not to do. The media content pulled at him-each video, each headline-and he consumed it compulsively, as if understanding the mechanisms of violence might somehow protect him from it. By evening, he was smoking on his apartment balcony, a habit he had quit two years ago, his hands shaking as he lit one cigarette after another.

The triggers multiplied after that. Similar cars in traffic made his jaw clench. A guest at the hotel complained about a stain on her sheets, and when her tone sharpened, Miguel felt the old panic rising-the sensation of being accused of something he could not control, could not explain away. He began to avoid reminders of the event deliberately: he stopped watching the news, asked coworkers not to discuss politics or crime, and felt a spike of dread whenever someone mentioned his past or asked casual questions about where he was from. But the avoidance itself seemed to amplify his vigilance. By avoiding conversations about the trauma, he found himself scanning strangers' faces more intently, reading threat into neutral expressions. An elderly man approached him in the hotel lobby asking for directions, and Miguel's heart raced; he could not explain why, exactly, but the stranger's slow approach felt predatory.

His nights became a cycle of fragmentation. He would wake at two or three in the morning, his body rigid, and creep through his apartment checking locks, ensuring windows were secure. The hypervigilance was exhausting but felt necessary-a price he paid for safety. When Rosa had still been around, her touch on his shoulder in the dark would have startled him into a defensive posture; she had learned not to wake him. Now, alone, even the unexpected sound of the ice maker would send adrenaline flooding through him. One evening, a coworker placed a hand on his back to get past him in the supply closet, and Miguel spun around with such force that he knocked over a shelf of cleaning bottles. The startle, the shame that followed, the certainty that his body was betraying him-all of it fed back into his sense that danger was everywhere.

The threat monitoring had become so consuming that it began to reshape his avoidance strategies. He stopped taking the bus to work, fearing the enclosed space and the strangers pressed around him, which meant he now spent money on rideshare apps he could barely afford. He avoided the hotel's break room when police officers came through for a training seminar, staying in the laundry room for hours, smoking cigarette after cigarette to manage the anxiety of their proximity. The smoking itself had become a ritual, a way to create distance between himself and the world, and it had begun to worry him-he was up to a pack a day, sometimes more. Yet every time he tried to stop, the urge to smoke returned with such force that it felt inseparable from his need to manage the constant low-level terror.

What brought Miguel to the clinic was not a single crisis but an accumulation: the isolation, the financial strain of avoiding situations, the knowledge that his body no longer felt like his own. He had been divorced for fourteen months, had no close friends in Phoenix, and had begun calling in sick to work more frequently. When the intake therapist asked what he most feared, he said quietly: "That I'll never feel normal again. That I'm going to lose this job too, and then there's nothing left."
